# 2 Chronicles 14 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Verse 1

**v. 1: “Then Abijah rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. And his son Asa reigned in his place, and in his days the land was at peace for ten years.”**

- The phrase “rested/slept with his fathers” is a biblical euphemism for dying and being buried in the royal tomb (Precept Austin). “The City of David” in the OT refers to Jerusalem, specifically where David conquered the stronghold of Zion and was buried (1 Kings 2:10). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary)
- Gill notes that the “ten years” of quiet were the first three years of Asa’s reign plus the first seven of Baasha’s (king of Israel), after which there was war between them all their days (1 Kings 15:32). The Targum says “the land of Israel,” but the Septuagint more correctly says “the land of Judah.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests one cause of the peace was the defeat Jeroboam and Israel had suffered at the hands of Abijah (2 Chronicles 13:18–20), and a league between Abijah and the king of Syria (1 Kings 15:19). It also raises the question of Asa’s age at accession — possibly as young as twelve — though the text shows no indication of a child-king; the matter remains moot. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/Charismatic) notes that Asa was more like his ancestor David in character than like his own father Abijah. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)

## Verse 2

**v. 2: “And Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.”**

- Gill simply cross-references 1 Kings 15:11. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary observes that the Hebrew is emphatic — “*the* good and *the* straight” — with the Authorized Version italicizing the first three words to show they are supplied. Martin Selman notes that “good” has been added to “right” (cf. 1 Kings 15:11), parallel with the description of Hezekiah (the phrase recurs only in 2 Chr 31:20). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Frederick Mabie (noted at Precept Austin) observes that Asa is the first post-divided-kingdom Judean king described as doing what is right in God’s eyes, and his reforms function as a precursor to later reformer kings like Hezekiah and Josiah. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary)

## Verse 3

**v. 3: “He removed the foreign altars and high places, shattered the sacred pillars, and chopped down the Asherah poles.”**

- Gill explains that the “altars of the strange gods” were those of the Zidonians, Ammonites, and Moabites remaining from Solomon’s time (1 Kings 11:7). He notes that the high places “built for idols” were removed, but those on which the true God was worshipped were not removed in his days (1 Kings 15:14). The “images” (מַצֵּבוֹת) were statues or pillars erected to idols, and the “groves” (אֲשֵׁרִים) were the wooden Asherah poles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary gives a detailed word study: the Hebrew for “images” is *matstseboth*, rendered “pillar(s)” twelve times and “image(s)” nineteen times in the AV. It argues that “groves” (LXX ἄλσος, Vulgate *lucus*) misleads; the word *Asherim* ultimately denotes Astarte or the planet Venus, represented by a wooden pillar or trunk — a Phoenician/Canaanite fertility emblem associated with Baal. The verbs of “cutting down” and “burning” confirm it was a carved wooden object, not a grove of trees. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Guzik adds that 1 Kings 15:12 notes Asa “banished the perverted persons from the land” — state-sanctioned homosexual idol-temple prostitutes introduced under Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:24). Asa’s father Abijah had not removed these, but Asa did. 1 Kings 15:13 tells of removing his grandmother Maachah from being queen mother because she had made an obscene image of Asherah — “It is in a man’s own family circle that his faithfulness is put fairly to the test” (Knapp). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)
- **Denominational note — Baptist/Reformed:** John Piper (Desiring God, Reformed Baptist) preaches that Asa’s reform is an example of trusting God rather than man. In a sermon titled “Asa’s Folly,” he recounts this early faithfulness as the backdrop for later warning: “God had proved to Asa in the past that when he trusted him, great things happened for his good.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly)

## Verse 4

**v. 4: “He commanded the people of Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to observe the law and the commandments.”**

- Gill says Asa did this “by a public edict” — to pray to the Lord alone, attend His worship, and observe all the laws: moral, ceremonial, and civil. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- Guzik notes that Asa could not force people to seek the LORD, but he could “command them with moral force and with his own example.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)
- The Pulpit Commentary observes that the word “commanded” indicates the moral (rather than purely physical-force) efforts of Asa — confirmatory that the high-place removal relied heavily on moral suasion. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Andrew Hill (at Precept Austin) notes that “seeking the LORD” occurs nine times in the three chapters covering Asa (14:4, 7 [2×]; 15:2, 4, 12, 13, 15; 16:12) — setting the theme for the entire section. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary)

## Verse 5

**v. 5: “He also removed the high places and incense altars from all the cities of Judah, and under him the kingdom was at peace.”**

- Gill distinguishes between the high places in v. 3 (those in and near Jerusalem) and those here in “all the cities of Judah.” He says the “images” (*chammanim*) were “sun images” — either made in the form of the sun, dedicated to it, or temples for it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew *chammanim* (here “incense altars” or “images”) occurs seven other times (Lev 26:30; 2 Chr 34:4, 7; Isa 17:8; 27:9; Ezek 6:4, 6). Gesenius connects it with Baal-Hammon, an epithet of Baal as sun-god. The objects may have been pyramid-shaped statues of the sun placed in Baal-temples. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- The kingdom’s quietness is directly tied to Asa’s reforms — peace as a reward for faithfulness, illustrating the Chronicler’s “retribution theology” (obedience brings blessing; disobedience brings punishment). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary)

## Verse 6

**v. 6: “Because the land was at peace, Asa built fortified cities in Judah. In those days no one made war with him, because the LORD had given him rest.”**

- Gill says Asa built (or rebuilt) fenced cities as defence against Israel and other nations, following Rehoboam’s earlier work (2 Chr 11:5) — these may have been demolished by Shishak (2 Chr 12:4–5). The rest was from the Lord so Asa could have leisure for reforms: “all rest is from the Lord, civil, spiritual, and eternal.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- Guzik quotes John Trapp: “Though he had no war, yet he provided for it. So did our Queen Elizabeth; and so must every Christian soldier.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)
- Precept Austin points out the balanced biblical pattern: trusting God’s sovereignty while taking personal responsibility (cf. Psalm 127:1: “Unless the LORD guards the city, the watchman keeps awake in vain”). Later in his reign Asa would rely on his own wisdom, but here he still relies on God. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary)

## Verse 7

**v. 7: “So he said to the people of Judah, ‘Let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, with doors and bars. The land is still ours because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought Him and He has given us rest on every side.’ So they built and prospered.”**

- Gill notes that Asa addressed “the nobles and principal men of the kingdom.” The phrase “while the land is yet before us” means no enemy is in it to hinder or molest. The cause of rest is explicitly stated: “because we have sought the LORD our God.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- Guzik observes that the Chronicler includes this building account (not in 1 Kings) to encourage his post-exilic readers who had been allowed to rebuild Jerusalem after the Babylonian destruction. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)
- Raymond Dillard notes that “building, prosperity, and the possession of the land depend on seeking God” — a message with homiletical relevance for the post-exilic community. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary)

## Verse 8

**v. 8: “Asa had an army of 300,000 men from Judah bearing large shields and spears, and 280,000 men from Benjamin bearing small shields and drawing the bow. All these were mighty men of valor.”**

- Gill describes the Judahites as armed with large shields (*tsinnah* — a full-body shield) and spears for close combat; the Benjaminites with smaller shields and bows for ranged attack. All were “able bodied men, valiant and courageous.” He suggests Asa gathered these upon hearing of the Ethiopian threat. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the minute historical coherence: Benjamin’s specialisation as archers matches 1 Chronicles 8:40, 12:2, and the ancient blessing of Genesis 49:27. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Total army: 580,000 — a substantial force, but as v. 9 will reveal, not enough against the coming threat without divine help. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)

## Verse 9

**v. 9: “Then Zerah the Cushite came against them with an army of 1,000,000 men and 300 chariots, and they advanced as far as Mareshah.”**

- Gill gives an extensive discussion of who Zerah was. Some say he was a Cushite Arab from Midian (near Judah), not an African Ethiopian — because the distance and passage through Egypt seemed implausible. However, since the host included Lubim (Libyans, Africans) per 2 Chronicles 16:8, Gill leans toward African Ethiopia, which controlled Egypt and Libya shortly after Shishak’s death. He defends the number by citing comparable ancient armies (Tamerlane’s 1,600,000, Bajazet’s 1,400,000). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary gives a detailed historical-geographical discussion: “Ethiopia” (Cush) broadly designated Nubia, Sennaar, Kordofan, and part of Abyssinia. It suggests Zerah may have been Usarken II (Osorkon II), fourth king of Egypt’s 22nd dynasty, making the invasion an Egyptian expedition with mercenary forces. The defeat of Zerah would explain the known decline of Egyptian power about 25–30 years after Shishak. However, it admits certainty is impossible. The army of “a thousand thousand” is the largest number given for any army in the OT. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Guzik cites Selman: “Zerah himself is most likely to have been a Nubian (= Sudanese) general in the army of Pharaoh Osorkon I (c. 924–884 B.C.), Shoshenq I’s son and successor.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)
- **Modern scholarship:** Gleason Archer (cited at Precept Austin) notes that no mention of Zerah has yet turned up outside the Bible. Kitchen dates the battle to about 897 B.C. and suggests Osorkon I (then elderly) may have sent a general of Nubian extraction — but Zerah was defeated, so no triumphal Egyptian relief exists. Archer argues that absence of extrabiblical attestation does not disprove historicity; many once-sceptically-viewed biblical names have been vindicated by archaeology. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary)

## Verse 10

**v. 10: “So Asa marched out against him and lined up in battle formation in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah.”**

- Gill notes Asa’s courage: despite the vast enemy host, “he did not stay till they got further into his country, but marched against them when on the frontiers of it, and chose the valley to pitch in, as being more to the advantage of his smaller army.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary discusses the Hebrew word for “valley” (*gê*’), which appears 56 times in the OT and is the word used in Psalm 23:4 (“valley of the shadow of death”) and Isaiah 40:4 (“every valley shall be exalted”). It is not necessarily a ravine but a low, flat region. Zephathah may relate to Zephath of Judges 1:17. Mareshah lay about one Roman mile south-west of modern Beit-Jibrin (Eleutheropolis). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)

## Verse 11

**v. 11: “Then Asa cried out to the LORD his God: ‘O LORD, there is no one besides You to help the powerless against the mighty. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on You, and in Your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, You are our God. Do not let a mere mortal prevail against You.’”**

- This is the theological centre of the chapter. Gill says Asa prayed “with vehemence, being in distress… before the battle began, at the head of his army, and for the encouragement of it.” The phrase “it is nothing with thee to help” means numbers make no difference to God (cf. 1 Samuel 14:6). “We rest on thee” — the Targum renders, “on thy Word we lean.” “Let not man prevail against thee” — because if the enemy prevailed against Judah, it would be interpreted as prevailing against their God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary analyses the prayer as “a model prayer to an omnipotent Deliverer”: it opens with invocation and the postulate of God’s omnipotence; repeats the invocation with the appropriating “our”; petitions “Help us”; argues from trusting dependence (“we rest on thee, and in thy Name we go against this multitude”); and closes with the clenching challenge of covenant relationship — “do not let mortal man prevail against You.” The Hebrew for “man” here is *’enosh*, a poetical, universal term emphasising frailty. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Guzik emphasises that Asa “recognized that this battle belonged to the LORD and called upon God to defend His honor.” He quotes F.B. Meyer: “Remind God of His entire responsibility.” Asa prayed not merely for victory but for God to defend His own reputation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)
- **Charismatic/Pentecostal application:** Guzik applies this to believers facing overwhelming odds — “we should follow Asa’s example by trusting in God’s power rather than our own strength, and by calling on Him to defend His honor in our situation.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** In his sermon “A Lesson from the Life of King Asa,” Spurgeon says: “How grandly he threw all his burden upon God! He declared that he rested in the Most High… after this prayer he marched to the battle with holy confidence, and God gave him the victory.” Yet Spurgeon immediately warns: “You would not have thought that a man who could perform that grand action would become, a little after, full of unbelief; but the greatest faith of yesterday will not give us confidence for today.” (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-lesson-from-the-life-of-king-asa)
- **Reformed Baptist (Piper):** John Piper calls this a model of hoping in God: “He humbled himself and hoped in God.” He cites this prayer to show that trusting God brings God’s powerful deliverance, while later Asa’s folly was trusting in man. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly)

## Verse 12

**v. 12: “So the LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and Judah, and the Cushites fled.”**

- Gill says the Lord smote the Ethiopians “with consternation and terror; they were thrown into a panic” — just as Jeroboam and Israel had fled in the preceding chapter (2 Chr 13:15). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary observes how little is said of the human method: “As little as the real work was of the army of Asa, so little is said of even the mere human method by which this great victory was obtained.” The glory is given repeatedly to “the LORD.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Guzik: “God fought on behalf of King Asa and the kingdom of Judah; He fought so effectively that they were broken before the LORD and His army.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)

## Verse 13

**v. 13: “Then Asa and his army pursued them as far as Gerar. The Cushites fell and could not recover, for they were crushed before the LORD and His army. So the people of Judah carried off a great amount of plunder.”**

- Gill notes that Gerar was a city of the Philistines (Genesis 20:1). The Cushites “were thrown into such a fright, and into so much confusion, that they could not put themselves in order, and rally again.” “Before the LORD and before his host” may refer to the army of Israel (with the LORD as its Commander), or to an host of angels — the Syriac and Arabic versions read “the angel of the Lord smote the Ethiopians.” Josephus says the plunder included much gold and silver. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary calculates Gerar was more than twenty miles from Mareshah, nearly four hours south of Gaza on the road to Egypt — showing the extent of the pursuit. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)
- Guzik: “Not only were the people of God delivered from this danger, they were also enriched when the LORD fought on their behalf. In this sense, they were more than conquerors in that the LORD did the fighting and they shared in the spoil” (echoing Romans 8:37). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)

## Verse 14

**v. 14: “and attacked all the cities around Gerar, because the terror of the LORD had fallen upon them. They plundered all the cities, since there was much plunder there.”**

- Gill says these were the cities of the Philistines, who were auxiliaries and confederates with the Ethiopians. “The fear of the LORD came upon them” — they had no power to defend themselves. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew word for “spoil” (*bizzah*) here is found only in Chronicles, Ezra, Esther, Nehemiah, Daniel, and once in Ezekiel (29:19) — a late Hebrew term. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/14.htm)

## Verse 15

**v. 15: “They also attacked the tents of the herdsmen and carried off many sheep and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.”**

- Gill identifies “the tents of cattle” as the dwellings of the Scenite Arabs — nomadic people living in tents for pasturage. The “sheep and camels in abundance” indicate the enormous wealth plundered. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-14.html)
- Guzik: Adam Clarke comments that “the spoil was immense, because the multitude was prodigious, indeed almost incredible; a million of men in one place is almost too much for the mind to conceive, but there may be some mistake in the numerals; it is evident from the whole account that the number was vast and the spoil great.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-14/)
- The chapter closes with a triumphant return to Jerusalem — the entire episode (vv. 9–15) forming a vivid, fast-moving battle narrative unique to Chronicles.

## Summary of Protestant Distinctives Observed

| Tradition | Emphasis |
|-----------|----------|
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik) | Stresses prayer as a weapon, God’s miraculous intervention, the Holy Spirit’s role in empowering believers to be “more than conquerors,” and personal application for spiritual warfare. |
| **Baptist** (Gill, Spurgeon) | Focus on the sovereignty of God in giving rest and victory; Gill provides precise historical-grammatical detail; Spurgeon highlights faith and warns that past faith does not guarantee future faithfulness. |
| **Reformed Baptist** (John Piper / Desiring God) | Emphasises God’s eagerness to show His power for those who trust Him wholly; sees Asa’s early reign as illustrative of the “retribution principle” and a foil for later self-reliance. Piper’s key text is 2 Chronicles 16:9 (“the eyes of the LORD run to and fro”). |
| **Reformed/Evangelical** (Precept Austin, Carson, Dillard, Duguid) | Highlights Chronicler’s “retribution theology” (obedience → blessing; disobedience → curse); the theme of “seeking the LORD”; covenantal rest as fulfilment of Deut 12:8–10. Emphasises that faithfulness must be learned anew in each circumstance. |
| **Anglican/Traditional Protestant** (Pulpit Commentary) | Detailed philological and historical notes; careful handling of apparent contradictions (high places); identifies prayer structure as a “model prayer to an omnipotent Deliverer.” |

## Other Views

- **Modern Scholarship (Historical-Critical):** The identity of Zerah remains unconfirmed outside the Bible. K.A. Kitchen dates the battle to c. 897 B.C. and suggests Zerah was a Nubian general under Pharaoh Osorkon I. Gleason Archer defends the historicity, noting that absence of external evidence does not equal falsehood and that many once-sceptically-viewed biblical names have been vindicated by archaeological discoveries. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-14-commentary)
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** No specific commentary pages on 2 Chronicles 14 were found from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits. The Catholic tradition would typically read this chapter within the context of the Deuteronomistic history, emphasising Asa’s cultic reform as prefiguring the Church’s ongoing call to purity of worship.
- **Prosperity/Word of Faith:** While not directly sourced, the chapter’s pattern of “seek God → receive rest, prosperity, and plunder” has sometimes been cited by prosperity teachers to link faithfulness with material blessing. The traditional commentaries above, however, uniformly interpret the “prosperity” and “plunder” as covenant blessings specific to the theocratic kingdom of Judah — not a universal promise of wealth.
